About us
We’re a team of computer science students who love AI, programming, and solving real problems together.

Why join our team?
We’re organized, open to everyone’s ideas, and focused on turning plans into working results. All levels are welcome, and everyone gets room to learn and contribute.

Skills we’re looking for
Programming or data skills, design and creativity, and good presentation. Most of all, someone curious and reliable who enjoys teamwork.
summary: A space mission is a chain of choices—and every kilogram matters. In Every Kilogram, players become mission designers, turning a science goal into a spacecraft that can travel, operate, and succeed within tight limits. They choose mission hardware and balance mass, power, cost, and capability, then launch the mission and see how those decisions shape its outcome. A mission review connects the experience to real mission segments, concepts of operations, and NASA missions, while short learning activities help players understand the reasoning behind each trade-off. The game addresses the Space Mission Design Challenge by making mission planning hands-on and approachable: players learn through building, testing, and revising instead of only reading about spacecraft. By showing how engineering decisions affect scientific goals, Every Kilogram helps turn the complexity of space exploration into an engaging learning experience.
details:
Every Kilogram’s Project Solution

We didn’t just build a spacecraft builder—we built a mission adventure where players make the choices, fly the mission, and discover what those choices mean. In Every Kilogram, the player joins a crew, picks a science goal, designs a spacecraft, and then sees whether it can bring the science home. The game makes a complicated idea simple to feel: every new instrument or capability affects the rest of the mission.

How Does Our Solution Work?

Players choose from missions to the Moon, Mars, Venus, and Europa, as well as Earth-orbit training flights. Before building, they decide what scientific result counts as success. Then they choose spacecraft parts and balance:

  • Mass and launch capacity: The rocket must be able to lift the spacecraft.
  • Power and time: The spacecraft needs enough energy to operate throughout the mission.
  • Data and communications: Collecting science is only useful if the spacecraft can store and send it home.
  • Budget and capability: More capable equipment can bring extra costs and trade-offs.



Players then launch and fly a short simulation, handle problems, and—on landing missions—explore the surface, scan science sites, and collect samples. After the flight, a mission review traces how design choices led to the result, compares the player’s spacecraft with a real mission, and offers a chance to fly again with a different design.

The Game Benefits

The game helps players learn by making decisions and seeing their consequences. It:

  • Connects a mission’s science goal to spacecraft requirements.
  • Makes engineering trade-offs visible through play.
  • Introduces mission phases, mission timelines, and real spacecraft examples.
  • Supports solo play and crew play, in English and Arabic.



Our Goal

We want students and curious players to understand how spacecraft design supports scientific discovery—and why a mission team has to balance many requirements at once. The simulation is simplified for learning and play; it is not a professional mission-design tool.

Tools and Technologies Used

  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the browser game.
  • Three.js for the 3D spacecraft, flight, and surface scenes.
  • Node.js for serving the game locally and supporting same-room multiplayer.
  • PeerJS and WebRTC for online play between players’ browsers.
  • NASA and USGS imagery, plus original characters and the KILO robot guide.

Data Sources

NASA and USGS references inform the game’s science, spacecraft, and simplified engineering models. Examples include:

  • NASA Glenn’s Beginner’s Guide to Aeronautics for the rocket equation and how added mass affects propellant.
  • NASA/NSSDC planetary fact sheets for planetary properties used in orbit and mission calculations.
  • NASA/JPL mission materials, including the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter press kit and Europa Clipper facts, for examples of spacecraft, instruments, power, and communications.
  • NASA’s Deep Space Network documentation for concepts behind sending data across distance.
  • NASA’s MMRTG fact sheet for the radioisotope power option.
  • JPL’s approximate planetary positions and NASA’s Trajectory Browser as references for planetary positions and launch windows.
  • NASA and USGS planetary imagery for the worlds players explore.

Some scenarios can also use NASA’s DONKI space-weather service when the game is online. Game values are intentionally simplified, and the game identifies its sources so players can explore them further.

What Makes It Creative, and What Did We Consider?

Players don’t just receive a score: the review presents a chain of cause and effect, showing how one choice led to another. They can adjust their design and fly again, turning failure into a new experiment. We considered scientific goals, spacecraft limits, player accessibility, language support, and the need for the game to run in a browser on typical school computers.
